title: Consistent Hashing
explain: Consistent hashing places servers and keys on the same ring, and each key belongs to the next server clockwise. When a server joins or leaves, only the keys next to it move — about 1/N of them — instead of almost all keys as with `hash mod N`. I use it when I want each key to stick to one server while the server count changes.
model:
```
0 ─────────────────────────────── 2^m − 1 (wraps)
A(10) ───── B(40) ───── C(80)           keys in (10,40] → B
A(10) ─ D(25) ─ B(40) ───── C(80)        D joins: only (10,25] moves, B → D
```

- **Virtual nodes:** each server takes many tokens so shares are even and a leaving server's load spreads over many neighbours.
- **Bounded load:** cap each node at ~1.25 × average and spill to the next node, to survive hot keys.
- **Scaling out — cache vs database:**
  - cache: no migration, moved keys just miss and refill;
  - database: new node joins as *joining* → copy its range while the old owner still serves → switch traffic → old owner deletes.

**Use it** for key affinity with a changing node set (caches, KV stores). **Don't** use it to route to stateful backends that own sessions or in-flight work — route those by an explicit owner lookup.

details.a: Changing N remaps almost every key (going from 4 to 5 nodes moves 80%). With a ring, adding one node moves about 1/(N+1).

With one token per node the arcs are uneven, so load is uneven, and a departing node dumps its whole arc on one neighbour. Many tokens per node make each share close to 1/N and spread failures; weights are just more tokens for bigger machines.

details.q: Which node takes over when D joins at 25 between A(10) and B(40)?
details.a: With 'the next token clockwise owns the key', D takes (10, 25] from B. Some systems use the opposite convention — say which one you use.

details.q: What about a single hot key?
details.a: Hashing cannot split one key. Use bounded-load hashing to spill traffic, replicate the hot key to several nodes, or cache it closer to clients.

details.q: Why not use it to route WebSocket sessions or running jobs?
details.a: A rebalance silently moves keys to new owners, but the state (the open connection, the in-flight job) stays on the old server. Those need an explicit registry of who owns what.

details.q: How does adding a database node differ from adding a cache node?
details.a: A cache can just miss and refill. A database must copy the range first and switch traffic only once the new node has caught up, or reads would return nothing.

prompts.q: Explain consistent hashing and why it beats `hash mod N`, with a quick sketch.
points: Nodes and keys on the same ring
A key goes to the next node clockwise
Adding a node moves only its arc (~1/N)
mod N moves almost everything when N changes

prompts.q: Walk through adding a node to a consistent-hashed database without losing reads.
points: The new node joins in a joining state
Its range is copied while the old owner keeps serving
Traffic switches once it has caught up
The old owner deletes its copy
Contrast: a cache can skip the copy

prompts.q: Say when you would and would not use consistent hashing.
points: Use: caches and KV stores that want key affinity
Use: the node count changes often
Don't: stateless requests that just need load balancing
Virtual nodes / bounded load for evenness and hot keys
